extracted.intended_audience: novelists and creative writers (especially those writing serialized novels or long-form fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical standards for writing novels (especially serialized or long-form) covering character development, plotting, publication habits, and audience targeting. Emphasises discipline, research, and handling magazine/serial publication issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression of character over time
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of progression in character,—of marking the changes in men and women which would naturally be produced by the lapse of years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-range or multi-volume works, plan and show how characters change with years and circumstances. Use long-term moral/psychological trajectories (good leads to good, evil leads to evil). Examples: the development of Violet Effingham, Lady Laura, and the hero in Trollope's novels; contrast with short-timeframe works where such progression is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency in short-timeframe novels
rubrics_metrics.description: In novels whose incidents occur in a short period (e.g., less than a month), characters should remain consistent throughout the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story's timeframe is brief (example: Ivanhoe), avoid retroactive changes in character — maintain single consistent characterisation across the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine politics with human-interest elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A tale cannot be made pleasing chiefly by politics; political writing must be combined with love and intrigue, social incidents, and perhaps a dash of sport to engage readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a politically minded protagonist, include romantic plots, social interactions, and incidental pleasures to broaden appeal — otherwise non-political readers will be alienated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience sensitivity to nationality and reader prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of choosing a hero whose nationality or background will make sympathy and affection difficult for the target readers (example: an Irish politician in England).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prevailing attitudes of your primary readership when selecting protagonists or cultural backgrounds; avoid unnecessarily alienating choices unless their awkwardness is a deliberate artistic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan endings and future possibilities (avoid irreversible encumbrances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make unconsidered choices (e.g., marrying a hero in a way that prevents future narrative developments); failing to plan an ending can force awkward solutions later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend to revisit characters or write sequels, leave options open in the plot and avoid decisions that box you into killing or otherwise removing characters to resolve narrative constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresee characters' moral trajectories
rubrics_metrics.description: Know 'the evil and the good of my puppets, and how the evil would always lead to evil, and the good produce good' — have clear moral trajectories for characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters with foreseeable tendencies so that their actions and consequences feel inevitable and coherent; this foreshadowing aids credibility and long-term plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct observation/research for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: To write convincingly about institutions or settings (e.g., the House of Commons), go and see them — obtain access/observation where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firsthand attendance/observation (e.g., securing a gallery seat to watch parliamentary proceedings) improves the accuracy and authority of scenes and mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain disciplined, artisan-like work habits
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional writer should be bound to rules of labour similar to those of an artisan or mechanic — keep producing rather than idling over a finished work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt regular writing routines: start the next work promptly after finishing one, keep a pen in hand habitually, and treat writing as continual production rather than intermittent inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuality and meeting publication exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: An author writing for periodicals is obliged to suit the exigencies of editors and must be punctual; Trollope claims never to have been a day late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor deadlines, supply the agreed amount and timing of material to publishers; reliability is a professional duty and prevents causing inconvenience to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle editorial and scheduling conflicts pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishers' schedules collide (e.g., another author's delay forcing a clash), negotiate but be prepared to refuse or adapt (e.g., publish in separate numbers or another periodical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance willingness to accommodate with defending your own position; sometimes partial concession (giving half) and refusing the rest is an equitable tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating sympathy for a flawed protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying a man led astray by his unwillingness to defer to others should create reader sympathy; failure to do so is a core narrative weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To engender sympathy for an unfortunate or morally compromised protagonist, show the human reasons for his errors, his inner struggles, and the consequences in ways that make the reader empathise rather than only judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of long intervals between parts/sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing a sequel after a long interval (e.g., six years) risks the original readers not remembering characters or interest fading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If planning sequels, consider continuous or reasonably timed publication, or include sufficient reintroduction material so returning readers can re-engage with characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely on subordinate characters to redeem a flawed main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel which in its main parts is bad cannot, in truth, be redeemed by the vitality of subordinate characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While strong minor characters are valuable, ensure the central plot and main characterisation are solid; secondary vitality is supplementary, not a cure for foundational weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to reader segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Different reader groups respond to different elements: politically conversant men may enjoy a parliamentary hero, while other readers (e.g., women interested in social and romantic plots) will prefer different focal points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know which audience segment you aim to satisfy and balance elements (politics, romance, social incident) to match their tastes if broad appeal is desired, or accept narrower appeal if focusing on a specific readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fiction as a vehicle for views when public speech is constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: If barred from expressing opinions publicly, an author can declare them through fiction (e.g., writing semi-political tales to express political ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage novelistic narrative as an indirect means to explore and advocate for political or social positions, embedding argument within character and plot rather than polemic.
